title: Score a text-to-SQL eval and read the hard slice
brief:
Your team wants to replace a frontier model with a small fine-tuned model for a text-to-SQL feature (see 1.3.2). Before anyone touches latency, the small model has to pass your evals (see 1.3.1). `eval_results.jsonl` holds 20 eval items, each tagged `easy` or `hard`, with the reference query and what each model wrote.

Write the scorer: normalise queries so cosmetic differences (case, spacing, a trailing semicolon) don't count as errors, then compute accuracy overall and per slice. Report the **small model's accuracy on the hard items**.

Python standard library only. The tests use their own tiny sample, so they won't give the answer away.
steps: Open `score_eval.py` and read the docstrings. `load_rows` and `main` are already written.
Implement `normalise_sql` following the four rules in its docstring.
Implement `accuracy`, including the optional `tag` filter and the ValueError cases.
Run `python -m pytest -q` until every test passes.
Run `python score_eval.py`. Read off the small model's hard-slice accuracy and compare it with its overall score.

solution.walkthrough:
**Normalise first.** Several of the small model's answers differ from the reference only cosmetically: q01 is lowercase with a semicolon, q03 has a double space and a line break, q08 has padding. After lowercasing, stripping, dropping trailing semicolons and collapsing whitespace they match, so all 12 easy items count as correct for both models.

**Hard items (q13 to q20), small model:**

| Item | Verdict | Why |
|---|---|---|
| q13 | correct | identical join and GROUP BY |
| q14 | wrong | filters an aggregate in WHERE instead of HAVING |
| q15 | correct | only a trailing semicolon differs |
| q16 | wrong | inner JOIN where a LEFT JOIN is needed, so it can never find unsold products |
| q17 | correct | only case differs |
| q18 | correct | identical, including ORDER BY |
| q19 | wrong | uses AVG() directly in WHERE instead of a subquery |
| q20 | correct | only a trailing semicolon differs |

That is 5 of 8, so the hard-slice accuracy is 5 ÷ 8 = **62.5%**.

**The full report:** the frontier model scores 95.0% overall and 87.5% on hard items (it drops the ORDER BY on q18). The small model scores 85.0% overall (17 of 20) and 100% on easy items.

**What it means.** The small model's 85% headline looks close to the frontier's 95%, but on the hard items, the ones the evals should focus on, it gets 62.5% against 87.5%. Its errors are real semantic mistakes (HAVING versus WHERE, join type, subqueries), not formatting. Before shipping it, you would add more hard items, fine-tune on labelled examples of these patterns, and re-run the eval. Also look at the data: lowercasing string literals is a shortcut that could hide a wrong filter value, and exact match marks some equivalent queries wrong, which is why real text-to-SQL evals often execute the queries and compare results.
